q: Rare steak is ordered and the guest asks for white wine rather than red. Which white gives the dish the best chance?
opts: A light, neutral white at eleven percent
A sweet botrytised white
A full-bodied white with oak and some grip
An off-dry aromatic white
exp: White wine carries far too little tannin to meet the protein the way a red does, so the match has to be made on weight and texture instead, and a barrel-aged white has both, with a little grip of its own from the oak. Anything light or sweet is simply flattened by the meat, and the guest concludes that white with steak cannot be done.

q: The same bird goes out four ways on tonight's menu. Which preparation calls for the fullest wine?
opts: Poached in a light stock
Roasted with the skin crisped and a pan gravy
Served cold and sliced into a salad
Steamed with ginger and spring onion, served plain
exp: Browning, crisp skin and a pan gravy add a weight and a savoury depth that gentle cooking never produces, so the same ingredient can end up needing a light white or a substantial red. That is why the protein named on the menu is such an unreliable guide on its own.

q: Beef carpaccio arrives sliced thin under lemon, oil and rocket rather than grilled. What happens to the wine choice?
opts: Much lighter and fresher
Unchanged, since the meat is the same
Heavier, since raw meat needs more tannin
Sweeter, to balance the bitterness of the rocket
exp: Raw, sliced thin and dressed with citrus and peppery leaves, the dish has far more in common with a first-course salad than with a grilled steak. Tannin has almost nothing to bind to, and the acid in the dressing is now the loudest thing on the plate.

q: A fiery Sichuan dish reaches the table and four bottles are already open. Which one will make the burn worse?
opts: A dry sparkling wine served very cold
A lightly sweet rose at eleven percent
An off-dry white at eight percent
A tannic red at fifteen percent
exp: Alcohol and tannin both sharpen the sensation of heat, so the strongest and grippiest bottle on the table is the one to keep well away from the chilli. Cold, low in alcohol and faintly sweet is the direction that helps, and all three of the others sit somewhere along it.

q: Ground black pepper crusts a steak thickly. Unlike chilli heat, what does this kind of spice allow?
opts: No wine at all, since pepper defeats every style
A very sweet wine, as with chilli
A dry red with savoury, peppery aromatics of its own
A wine as low in alcohol as possible
exp: The compound behind chilli sets off a genuine heat response that alcohol makes worse; the one behind black pepper is far milder and reads as an aroma as much as a burn. Peppery reds echo it happily, which is why a coarse-ground pepper crust is one of the easiest things on any menu to pour against.

q: Coconut milk softens a hot curry, and the dish is now rich as well as fiery. What does the coconut change about the recommendation?
opts: The dish no longer needs any sweetness in the glass
The dish is now best served with a dry oaked red
The wine can be as tannic as you like
The wine now needs weight as well as sweetness
exp: Fat coats the palate and takes some of the sting out of chilli, but it also adds body, so a wispy low-alcohol white that would have suited a thin broth is now too slight for the bowl. Something with a little sugar and a little more substance holds both ends of the dish.

q: The ice bucket comes out before the bottle has even been chosen, because the main course is fiercely hot. What is the chill doing for the guest?
opts: Lowering the wine's alcohol by a degree or so
Cooling the palate against the burn
Adding sweetness to the wine
Removing the tannin from the wine
exp: Temperature is the one lever a server still controls at the moment of service, and a well-chilled glass is a genuine relief beside chilli. Nothing in the bucket alters what is in the bottle, only how it is perceived, which is enough to rescue a difficult course.

q: Wasabi, mustard and horseradish all sting, and yet they behave quite differently from chilli at the table. What is the practical difference?
opts: They cannot be tasted alongside wine at all, at any strength
They are far hotter than any chilli
They make a wine taste sweeter
Their heat fades in seconds rather than building
exp: The volatile compounds behind mustard heat clear quickly and travel up the nose rather than settling on the tongue, so they disrupt a wine far less than capsaicin does. A dish seasoned with them can take a drier and stronger wine than a chilli dish of the same apparent intensity.

q: Grilled radicchio and bitter chicory leaves are the side dish. Which glass is least likely to turn harsh?
opts: A young red with drying, mouth-puckering tannin
A dry red fortified wine
A heavily oaked white
A soft red with very little tannin
exp: Bitterness in the glass adds to bitterness on the plate instead of cancelling it, so tannin and heavy oak both make bitter leaves worse. A soft fruity red or a fresh unoaked white leaves the vegetable to speak for itself, which is what the cook intended.

q: Peas, broad beans and a fistful of fresh herbs dominate a spring plate. Which white shares that green character rather than fighting it?
opts: A sweet Muscat
An oxidative, nutty dry white
A rich Chardonnay matured in new oak barrels
A herbaceous, unoaked Sauvignon Blanc
exp: This is one of the few places where an obviously green, grassy wine is an advantage rather than a liability, because the same character is already on the plate. A big oaked white buries the vegetables and a sweet one turns the whole dish into something else.

q: A deep, savoury mushroom and Parmesan risotto is going out. Which red is the safer recommendation?
opts: A tannic red aged in new oak
A mature, gentle red
A young red at the height of its grip
A sweet fortified red
exp: Savoury depth of this kind makes firm tannin read harder and drier than it really is, so age and gentleness matter far more than power. A red past its youth has already shed most of the grip that would clash, which is one of the few genuine arguments for opening an older bottle with a vegetarian dish.

q: Aubergine, courgette and peppers are stewed down in olive oil and served warm. Which is the natural pour?
opts: A powerful red at fifteen percent, aged in oak
A dry rose or a light red served cool
A sweet late-harvest wine
A heavily oaked white
exp: Olive oil and long, slow cooking give these vegetables a weight no salad has, and nothing like the depth a meat dish brings. The plate therefore sits in the gap between white-wine and red-wine territory rather than squarely in either. Rose and a lightly chilled red both live in that gap, which is much of why they suit a Mediterranean table.

q: Before a single bottle is opened, which of these vegetable dishes is already the friendliest to wine?
opts: A bowl of raw fennel and celery
A raw onion and tomato salad
Roasted root vegetables
Raw asparagus spears with a lemon dressing
exp: Heat, browning and concentrated sugar move a vegetable towards the wine; raw, green and pungent moves it away. The distinction is worth more to a beginner than any list of grape varieties, because it explains why the same vegetable can be easy company one night and impossible the next.

q: Six oysters, shucked and set on ice with nothing but a wedge of lemon. Which of these bottles is the classic pour?
opts: Meursault
A ripe New World Chardonnay
Chablis
An oaked white Rioja
exp: All four are made from grapes that can give a broad, rich wine, and the one that works is the one usually left alone in steel: little or no oak, no sweetness, high acid, and a saline edge that reads as an extension of the oyster. The grand cru bottles do see some barrel, but the everyday Chablis that goes with oysters does not, and oak with shellfish is one of the reliably bad combinations in the whole subject.

q: A whole side of salmon is grilled over coals and the table asks for red. Which grape is the standard answer?
opts: Nebbiolo
Cabernet Sauvignon
Tannat
Pinot Noir
exp: A red with low tannin and bright acidity behaves much like a white against fish, and salmon has enough oil and flesh to carry it. The big, structured reds are the ones usually blamed for the tinny taste fish is famous for causing, which is reason enough to keep them back for the meat course.

q: A stew has spent the afternoon cooking with the best part of a bottle of red wine in it. Which pour is the safest?
opts: A very old and delicate red, for its complexity
A dry sparkling wine, to lift the richness
A wine of the same style as the one in the pot
A sweet white, for contrast with the savoury stew
exp: Cooking with a wine and drinking it alongside is the oldest shortcut in pairing, and it works because the flavours in the pot are already the flavours in the glass. It is also the reason regional cooking and regional wine agree so often, since neither was developed with the other absent.
